Accustomed as an adjective carries the idea of familiarity built through habit or repeated experience. Something that is accustomed is not new, not surprising, and not uncomfortable — it has become normal.

The word works in two distinct ways depending on where it sits in a sentence, and understanding both will give you the complete picture.
Use 1: "Accustomed to something" — familiar through habit

When you say someone is accustomed to something, you mean they have experienced it so many times that it has become a natural, normal part of their life. It no longer shocks, bothers, or surprises them. They have adjusted to it.

Think of it this way: the first time you wake up at 5 AM, it feels brutal. But after doing it every day for a year, your body just does it. You are now accustomed to waking up early.

Some examples:

"She is accustomed to living alone." — Living alone is not strange for her. It's her normal.

"He is not accustomed to being criticized." — Criticism feels unfamiliar and uncomfortable to him. It's not something he normally experiences.

"The soldiers were accustomed to harsh conditions." — They had endured tough conditions so long that it no longer felt extreme to them.

Notice the structure: accustomed to + noun or verb(-ing). The "to" here is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, so the verb that follows it always ends in -ing. You say "accustomed to waking up early," never "accustomed to wake up early."

Becoming accustomed — this is important. You can also use the word to describe the process of getting used to something, not just the end state.

"It took her months to become accustomed to the city's noise." — She wasn't immediately comfortable; it happened gradually over time.

"You will soon grow accustomed to the new routine." — Familiarity will come with time.

Not yet accustomed — you can also use it to describe unfamiliarity, when the adjustment hasn't happened yet.

"I am still not accustomed to the cold here." — The cold still feels unusual or hard to cope with.
Use 2: Before a noun — usual, typical, or characteristic

This is a different but equally important use. When "accustomed" comes before a noun (not followed by "to"), it means usual, habitual, or characteristically typical of someone or something. It describes something that is expected and consistent because it happens regularly.

"She greeted everyone with her accustomed warmth." — This means her usual warmth — the warmth she always shows. It's what people expect from her.

"He completed the report with accustomed efficiency." — With his characteristic, typical efficiency. Just as he always does.

"The meeting began with the accustomed formalities." — The usual formalities that always happen at such meetings.

Here, "accustomed" is doing the job of words like usual, typical, customary, or characteristic. It carries a slight additional layer — not just that something is usual, but that it is usual because it has always been that way. There's a sense of established pattern behind it.
How the two uses relate to each other

They share the same root idea — habit and familiarity — but they point in different directions.

In "accustomed to", the focus is on a person and their familiarity with an experience. It answers the question: Has this person adjusted to this experience?

In "accustomed + noun", the focus is on a thing or quality, describing it as usual or typical. It answers the question: Is this their normal way of doing things?

These two expressions are very close in meaning, and in most everyday situations, they can be used interchangeably. "I am used to the noise" and "I am accustomed to the noise" mean the same thing. However, "accustomed" is noticeably more formal than "used to." You'll find "accustomed" more often in written English, in literature, in formal speech, and in professional contexts. "Used to" is the go-to choice in casual conversation.

The opposite of accustomed is unaccustomed, meaning unfamiliar with something or not in the habit of doing something. It follows the same logic.

"He was unaccustomed to failure." — Failure was foreign to him; he rarely experienced it.

"With unaccustomed shyness, she looked away." — She was shy in that moment, which was unusual for her.
The one thing to always remember

If you ever need to anchor the word to a single idea, remember this: accustomed = made normal by habit and repetition. Whether something has become normal for a person (accustomed to), or whether something is someone's normal (their accustomed way), the idea of repeated experience creating familiarity is always at the center.
